title: A $10 Chip Could Put a Lab on Your Wrist
summary:
Imagine checking your blood sugar with no needle, just a sensor on your wrist. Researchers at the University of Cambridge and a start-up called GlitterinTech built a chip that could one day make that possible. It costs just $10.

The chip reads light to learn what a substance is made of. Tools like this are called spectrometers. They are used in medicine, factories, food testing and nature studies. Big spectrometers work well, but making them small usually makes them less exact. This chip is only a few centimeters wide, yet the team says it is as precise as much bigger lab machines.

In tests, the chip correctly named plastics, medicines, coffee, flour and tea every time. It also measured health markers such as blood glucose, without needles, in one test over a long period. The researchers say much more testing is needed before it can become a real medical product.

The chip kept working from -20°C to 80°C, so it could suit wearables, factories and outdoor sensors.
why_it_matters: If it passes more tests, a wrist sensor could one day let kids check health markers without a needle.
